distillation_scope: Pure disease-name first-layer leaf distillation for TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome. This leaf models the full clinical manifold of TRAPS without adding genotype, penetrance, age, trigger, amyloidosis, or severity qualifiers to the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: TNFR1 misfolding and abnormal signaling activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: TNFRSF1A-related TNFR1 structural or shedding dysfunction lowers the threshold for recurrent sterile innate immune activation.
Downstream IL-1 beta, IL-6, neutrophilic inflammation, and oxidative stress produce fever, leukocytosis, CRP/SAA elevation, anemia of inflammation, and fatigue.
TRAPS flares commonly last more than a week, recur irregularly, and may leave subclinical inflammatory activity between attacks.
Sterile peritoneal, mesenteric, bowel-wall, and motility-related inflammation produces abdominal pain, constipation, colitis-like symptoms, ascites, obstruction mimics, and surgical-abdomen exposure.
Fascial, muscular, and dermal inflammation produces migratory myalgia, myositis/fasciitis, arthralgia or arthritis, and erythematous or vasculitic-appearing rash.
Orbital, conjunctival, and uveal inflammation can produce periorbital edema, conjunctivitis, ocular pain, or uveitis during flares.
Pleural, pericardial, and rare myocardial inflammation causes pleuritic pain, effusions, pericarditis, tamponade risk, dyspnea, or myocarditis-like severe presentations.
Repeated or persistent SAA elevation can drive systemic AA amyloid deposition, especially when inflammation is uncontrolled for years.
Renal AA amyloid deposition produces proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia, edema, progressive renal failure, dialysis need, and transplant exposure.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: TNFR1 dysfunction converges on IL-1/IL-6 dominated innate inflammation in many TRAPS phenotypes.
Germline TNFRSF1A biology creates the recurrent prolonged attack pattern.
The attack gate is observed clinically as recurrent prolonged inflammatory fever episodes.
TRAPS attacks usually last days to weeks rather than short hours-only flares.
Recurrent fever history is a core expression of the disease manifold.
Pyrogenic cytokines raise measured temperature during attacks.
Systemic cytokine activity produces malaise and functional impairment.
CRP rises with acute-phase activity.
SAA is a sensitive acute-phase marker and the substrate for AA amyloid.
ESR rises during attacks and chronic inflammation.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is common during flares.
The leukocytosis is often neutrophil-predominant.
Fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein elevated in inflammatory flares.
Inflammation and renal disease can lower hemoglobin.
Abdominal pain is a frequent TRAPS manifestation from serosal, mesenteric, bowel-wall, or myofascial inflammation.
Bowel-wall inflammation, pain, and dysmotility can produce constipation or delayed transit.
Severe inflammatory dysmotility or amyloid involvement can lead to obstruction-like presentations.
Mesenteric lymphadenitis can accompany pediatric inflammatory abdominal attacks.
Reactive ascites can accompany peritoneal inflammation or nephrotic hypoalbuminemia.
Focal or migratory myalgia is a classic TRAPS clue.
TRAPS can show inflammatory fasciitis or myositis in painful regions.
Joint pain commonly accompanies systemic flares.
Some patients have inflammatory arthritis during or between attacks.
Migratory erythematous plaques or patches overlying painful muscle groups are characteristic when present.
Periorbital edema is a recognized TRAPS manifestation.
Conjunctival inflammation can accompany ocular TRAPS flares.
Uveitis is uncommon but reported in TRAPS-spectrum inflammatory attacks.
Pleural serositis produces pleuritic pain.
Pericarditis is a recognized cardiopulmonary TRAPS manifestation.
Pericardial inflammation can produce effusion and rarely tamponade.
Pleural inflammation can produce effusion.
Persistent or repeated SAA elevation drives cumulative AA amyloid deposition risk.
Longstanding SAA exposure raises clinically meaningful AA amyloidosis hazard.
Kidney is a common dominant organ affected by AA amyloid in TRAPS.
Proteinuria is often the earliest renal amyloid clue.
Renal amyloid can produce nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and edema marks nephrotic renal amyloid.
Nephrotic protein loss and inflammation lower albumin.
Hypoalbuminemia and kidney disease cause peripheral edema.
Progressive renal amyloid lowers kidney function and raises creatinine.
Advanced renal amyloid can progress to dialysis or transplant-level kidney failure.
Large inflammatory pericardial effusions can rarely cause tamponade.

axes.shape_free_text: Recurrent, sterile, prolonged inflammatory fever attacks with well intervals or chronic low-grade activity between attacks.
Duration of the current or typical TRAPS inflammatory attack; often more than 6 days and sometimes several weeks.
Multiple relatives across generations with recurrent fever, abdominal pain, arthritis, serositis, amyloid, or similar unexplained inflammatory attacks.
Measured body temperature during an attack.
Reported fever burden across current or prior attacks.
Heart rate during fever, pain, anemia, or serositis.
Mean arterial pressure; usually preserved but can rise with kidney disease or fall with severe systemic inflammation.
Fatigue, malaise, or functional limitation during inflammatory activity.
Growth failure, poor weight gain, or chronic inflammatory undernutrition in pediatric disease.
Abdominal pain from sterile peritoneal, mesenteric, bowel-wall, or abdominal-wall myofascial inflammation.
Constipation, decreased stool output, or delayed bowel transit during gastrointestinal involvement.
Clinical or imaging obstruction, severe ileus, obstructive constipation, or surgical bowel-obstruction exposure.
Mesenteric lymphadenitis during abdominal inflammatory attacks.
Reactive ascites from serositis or nephrotic hypoalbuminemia.
Muscle pain during inflammatory attacks.
Focal migratory myalgia or painful myofascial inflammation that moves between limbs, trunk, or abdominal wall.
Imaging or clinical myositis/fasciitis in painful regions during TRAPS inflammation.
Joint pain during attacks or chronic inflammatory activity.
Objective inflammatory arthritis or recurrent arthritis episodes.
Migratory erythematous patches, plaques, papules, or rash overlying painful inflamed tissue.
Periorbital edema from orbital or systemic inflammation during TRAPS attacks.
Conjunctival inflammation during ocular TRAPS flares.
Anterior or other uveitis activity when present in TRAPS-spectrum ocular inflammation.
Throat pain, pharyngitis, or tonsillitis during flares; more common in pediatric presentations and not required.
Cervical, inguinal, mesenteric, or generalized lymphadenopathy during inflammatory activity.
Pleuritic chest pain during pleural or chest-wall inflammatory attacks.
Clinical or imaging-supported pericardial inflammation in TRAPS.
Pericardial effusion from pericardial serositis.
Pleural effusion from pleural serositis or nephrotic/systemic inflammation.
C-reactive protein during flare or persistent subclinical inflammation.
Serum amyloid A acute-phase concentration; persistent elevation drives AA amyloid risk.
ESR during flare or chronic inflammatory burden.
Peripheral leukocyte count during flare.
Absolute neutrophil count during neutrophilic flare.
Neutrophil fraction during inflammatory flare.
Hemoglobin; may be low with chronic inflammation or renal amyloid disease.
Ferritin can rise as an acute-phase marker but is not required for TRAPS.
Fibrinogen as an acute-phase protein.
Serum albumin; falls with nephrotic protein loss or inflammation.
Serum creatinine; usually normal in uncomplicated flares and elevated with renal amyloidosis or kidney failure.
Blood urea nitrogen; rises with renal amyloid, dehydration, or kidney failure.
Detectable proteinuria, especially from renal AA amyloid.
Quantified 24-hour urine protein; nephrotic-range values are common with renal amyloidosis.
Composite nephrotic presentation with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and often hyperlipidemia.
Leg, generalized, or nephrotic edema from renal amyloid or hypoalbuminemia.
Daily hazard of clinically meaningful AA amyloid deposition from persistent SAA exposure in TRAPS.
Daily hazard of progression to end-stage kidney disease from renal amyloidosis or severe chronic renal damage.
Daily hazard of hemodynamically significant pericardial tamponade from inflammatory effusion.
Need to adjust medication dosing or monitoring for kidney impairment or dialysis/transplant context.
Concurrent serious infection context that changes the safety of IL-1 blockade, TNF blockade, or glucocorticoids.
Any barrier that limits persistence with biologic treatment, including tolerance, adherence, access, cost, or administration logistics.

Lifespan outcome hazard for TRAPS, usually low with controlled inflammation but rising with systemic AA amyloidosis, ESKD, severe cardiopulmonary serositis, tamponade, bowel ischemia, or diagnostic delay.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP are jointly driven by cytokine flare activity.
CRP and SAA are coupled acute-phase reactants.
TRAPS leukocytosis is usually neutrophil-predominant during flares.
Migratory focal pain is a satellite pattern of myalgia.
Imaging myositis or fasciitis is the tissue correlate of severe myofascial pain.
Mesenteric lymphadenitis can accompany abdominal inflammatory attacks, especially in children.
Pericardial inflammation and effusion commonly move together when this complication appears.
Cumulative SAA exposure drives AA amyloid hazard.
Heavy proteinuria is central to nephrotic syndrome.
Sustained renal amyloid nephrotic disease increases kidney-failure hazard.
Large or rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion can transition to tamponade.
ESKD is a major downstream contributor to TRAPS mortality risk.

treatments.clinical_role: Rapid IL-1 pathway suppression for active TRAPS inflammation, recurrent flares, or amyloid-risk inflammatory activity.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Blocking IL-1 signaling can rapidly lower fever and acute-phase activity.
Reducing inflammation lowers SAA and amyloid-driving substrate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Serious infection must be handled before or during cytokine blockade decisions.
Anakinra is renally cleared and requires dosing adjustment in severe kidney impairment.
Daily injections, local reactions, or access barriers can limit durable response.

treatments.clinical_role: Longer-acting IL-1 beta suppression for sustained flare prevention and acute-phase control when ongoing biologic suppression is needed.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: IL-1 beta neutralization suppresses inflammatory attack activity.
Sustained acute-phase suppression reduces amyloidogenic exposure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Longer-acting biologic suppression is risky when serious infection is active.
Access or administration barriers can prevent sustained dosing.

treatments.clinical_role: TNF-pathway modulation that can reduce attacks in some TRAPS patients but may leave residual SAA or fail in others.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: TNF modulation can partially reduce flare activity in selected patients.
Residual SAA elevation may persist despite symptom improvement.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TNF modulation changes infection safety tradeoffs.

treatments.clinical_role: Temporary suppression of acute attack symptoms and inflammation; repeated dependence does not substitute for durable control of SAA exposure.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Glucocorticoids can abort or blunt flares in many patients.

treatments.display_name: NSAIDs, antipyretics, analgesia, and hydration support
treatments.clinical_role: Symptom and physiology support during attacks while disease-shaping anti-inflammatory therapy is considered.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Antipyretics lower temperature without resolving the disease manifold.
Analgesia reduces perceived pain and dehydration physiology.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: NSAIDs may be unsafe with renal amyloidosis, nephrotic syndrome, or kidney failure.

treatments.display_name: Renal amyloidosis, nephrotic, and CKD management
treatments.clinical_role: Nephrology management for proteinuria, nephrotic edema, hypertension, kidney failure, dialysis, and transplant while inflammatory control continues.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Diuresis, salt restriction, and nephrotic care reduce edema.
Kidney-protective management and renal replacement planning reduce complication hazard but do not erase amyloid biology.

treatments.display_name: Kidney replacement or transplant for TRAPS amyloidosis
treatments.clinical_role: Renal replacement therapy or transplantation for advanced TRAPS-related ESKD, paired with ongoing inflammation suppression to limit recurrent amyloid.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Renal replacement and transplant reduce uremic mortality risk in advanced kidney failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Transplant and dialysis infection contexts change timing and safety.

present.clinical_rationale: Confirmed TNFRSF1A context strongly supports the manifold, but genetic testing should stay confirmatory unless the runtime mode includes diagnostic workup evidence.
High-penetrance structural variants are associated with earlier onset, stronger inflammation, and higher amyloid risk.
Low-penetrance variants can still fit TRAPS when clinical criteria and prolonged attacks support the manifold, but expression is variable.
Dominant family clustering of prolonged inflammatory attacks raises prior probability when presentation fits.
Early onset with years of diagnostic delay increases cumulative inflammatory exposure and amyloid risk.
Ongoing acute-phase activity is the pathway from recurrent attacks to AA amyloidosis.
Nephrotic or renal amyloid context reshapes the disease toward chronic renal complication axes.
Concurrent infection can mimic TRAPS flares and changes treatment safety rather than becoming a TRAPS subtype.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Document attack duration, recurrence, well intervals, fever, abdominal/chest/muscle/skin/eye sites, and family history while still evaluating sepsis, appendicitis, IBD, vasculitis, malignancy, AOSD, FMF, MKD, CAPS, pericarditis, and true surgical abdomen when presentation warrants.
Trend CRP/SAA and monitor urinalysis, urine protein, albumin, creatinine, blood pressure, and edema because subclinical inflammation and proteinuria drive long-term amyloid risk.

Use genetic counseling and family assessment after clinical suspicion is established; do not let genotype or family segregation substitute for observed presentation evidence in presentation-only ranking.
Screen for infection and track injection reactions, adherence, access barriers, renal dosing, and vaccination or immunosuppression context around biologic therapy.
Coordinate renal amyloid, nephrotic, dialysis, transplant, pericarditis, effusion, and severe gastrointestinal complication care while treating the inflammatory driver.

quality_notes: No hand-authored treatment priority or expected-diagnosis labels are used.
The only derived_hazard axis is mortality_hazard_in_D-TRAPS.
Genotype, biopsy confirmation, final diagnosis, and treatment response should stay confirmatory/non-ranking in presentation-only cases unless a post-workup mode is explicitly used.
